introduction_markdown:
**Time allowed: three hours.** Answer ALL the SIX questions in this booklet. The mark allocation is indicated for each question. Each question carries 20 marks. Verify that this booklet contains six questions, no questions are repeated and there are no blank pages. Blank spaces in this question booklet may be used for rough work. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. All necessary working must be shown. No marks will be awarded for answers without brief statements showing how the answers have been obtained. Calculators may be used.

**Useful data:** relative atomic masses (RAM): C = 12.0, O = 16.0, H = 1.0, Al = 27.0, S = 32.0, Na = 23.0, Fe = 56.

The paper is arranged in three sections: Section A - Physical and General Chemistry; Section B - Inorganic Chemistry; Section C - Organic Chemistry.

questions.corrige_markdown:
| | Reagent(s) | Reaction conditions |
|---|---|---|
| (i) | Potassium (or sodium) cyanide, KCN, in ethanol (aqueous ethanolic solution) | Heat under reflux |
| (ii) | Dilute hydrochloric acid (or dilute sulphuric acid) | Heat under reflux (acid hydrolysis of the nitrile; with aqueous NaOH it would give the carboxylate, to be acidified) |
| (iii) | Aqueous sodium (or potassium) hydroxide, then dilute acid | Warm / heat under reflux, then acidify to free the acid |
| (iv) | Aqueous sodium (or potassium) hydroxide | Heat under reflux |

Reasoning: step (i) lengthens the carbon chain by one carbon, $\mathrm{C_2H_5Br} + \mathrm{CN^-} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CN} + \mathrm{Br^-}$; step (ii) is $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CN} + 2\mathrm{H_2O} + \mathrm{H^+} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CO_2H} + \mathrm{NH_4^+}$; step (iii) replaces the chlorine of $\mathrm{CH_3CHClCO_2H}$ (N) by OH: $\mathrm{CH_3CHClCO_2H} + \mathrm{OH^-} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CO_2H} + \mathrm{Cl^-}$ (in practice the acid is neutralised by the base, so one more mole of alkali is used, then the mixture is acidified); step (iv) is the substitution $\mathrm{C_2H_5Br} + \mathrm{OH^-} \rightarrow \mathrm{C_2H_5OH} + \mathrm{Br^-}$.

questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Names.**

| Compound | Formula | Name |
|---|---|---|
| M | $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CN}$ | propanenitrile (ethyl cyanide) |
| O | $\mathrm{CH_3CHO}$ | ethanal (acetaldehyde) |
| P | $\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CO_2H}$ | 2-hydroxypropanoic acid (lactic acid) |

(N, the intermediate in step (iii), is 2-chloropropanoic acid, $\mathrm{CH_3CHClCO_2H}$.) M is deduced because step (ii) gives $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CO_2H}$ (three carbons) from $\mathrm{C_2H_5Br}$ (two carbons): a nitrile hydrolyses to the acid with the same number of carbons. O comes from the oxidation of a primary alcohol with acidified dichromate under distillation, and it reacts with HCN (from $\mathrm{NaCN/H_2SO_4}$) to give $\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CN}$, so it is the aldehyde.

**(ii) Types of reaction.**

- Step (i): **nucleophilic substitution** (the nucleophile $\mathrm{CN^-}$ replaces $\mathrm{Br^-}$ on the carbon of the halogenoalkane).
- Step (v): **nucleophilic addition** (the cyanide ion adds to the $\mathrm{C{=}O}$ group of ethanal to give the hydroxynitrile / cyanohydrin).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) By means of a chemical test, how would you distinguish the following pairs of compounds. State reagents and reaction conditions.

(i) propanal and propanone

(ii) Ethene and Ethyne *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Propanal and propanone.** Add **Tollens' reagent** (ammoniacal silver nitrate, $\mathrm{[Ag(NH_3)_2]^+}$) and **warm in a water bath** at about $60\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. **Propanal**, an aldehyde, is oxidised to propanoate and gives a **silver mirror** (grey/black precipitate of silver); **propanone**, a ketone, gives **no reaction**:

$\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CHO} + 2[\mathrm{Ag(NH_3)_2}]^{+} + 3\mathrm{OH^-} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH_2COO^-} + 2\mathrm{Ag} + 4\mathrm{NH_3} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}$

(Alternative: warm with Fehling's or Benedict's solution; propanal gives a brick-red precipitate of copper(I) oxide, propanone does not. Both compounds react with 2,4-DNPH, so that reagent cannot distinguish them.)

**(ii) Ethene and ethyne.** Bubble each gas through **ammoniacal silver nitrate** (Tollens' reagent) at room temperature (or ammoniacal copper(I) chloride). **Ethyne**, a terminal alkyne with an acidic hydrogen, gives a **white precipitate of silver dicarbide (silver acetylide)**, $\mathrm{AgC{\equiv}CAg}$ (a **red precipitate** with copper(I) chloride):

$\mathrm{HC{\equiv}CH} + 2[\mathrm{Ag(NH_3)_2}]^{+} \rightarrow \mathrm{AgC{\equiv}CAg} + 2\mathrm{NH_4^+} + 2\mathrm{NH_3}$

**Ethene** gives **no precipitate**. (Bromine water cannot be used: both gases decolourise it.) The dry silver acetylide is explosive and must be destroyed with dilute acid after the test.

questions.enonce_markdown: (d) Outline the mechanism for the conversion of benzene to methylbenzene *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
The conversion is a **Friedel-Crafts alkylation**, a case of **electrophilic substitution**.

Reagents and conditions: chloromethane, $\mathrm{CH_3Cl}$, with **anhydrous aluminium chloride**, $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$ (halogen carrier catalyst), under dry conditions at room temperature or with gentle warming.

**Step 1 - formation of the electrophile:** $\mathrm{CH_3Cl} + \mathrm{AlCl_3} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH_3^{+}} + \mathrm{AlCl_4^{-}}$

**Step 2 - attack on the ring:** the $\pi$ electron system of benzene (curly arrow from the ring to the electrophile) attacks $\mathrm{CH_3^{+}}$ and forms a bond to carbon, giving a positively charged intermediate, the arenium ion ($\sigma$ complex), in which the carbon that has just bonded to $\mathrm{CH_3}$ is $sp^3$ and still carries its hydrogen, and the positive charge is delocalised over the other five ring carbons (the aromatic stability is temporarily lost).

**Step 3 - loss of a proton:** $\mathrm{AlCl_4^{-}}$ removes the $\mathrm{H^{+}}$ from the carbon bearing the methyl group (curly arrow from the C-H bond back into the ring), restoring the aromatic ring and regenerating the catalyst:

$\mathrm{C_6H_5(H)(CH_3)^{+}} + \mathrm{AlCl_4^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5CH_3} + \mathrm{HCl} + \mathrm{AlCl_3}$

Overall: $\mathrm{C_6H_6} + \mathrm{CH_3Cl} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{AlCl_3}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CH_3} + \mathrm{HCl}$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(e) 2-aminopropanoic acid $(\mathrm{CH_3CH(NH_2)CO_2H})$ is amphoteric in nature.

(i) Write chemical equations to show the reaction of 2-aminopropanoic acid with:

A- $\mathrm{HNO_3(aq)}$

B- $\mathrm{NaOH(aq)}$

(ii) Give the structure and general name of 2-aminopropanoic acid when in a neutral solution of pH = 7.

- Structure
- Name

(iii) Draw the stereo isomers of 2-aminopropanoic acid. *[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
2-aminopropanoic acid (alanine) has a basic amino group, $\mathrm{{-}NH_2}$, and an acidic carboxyl group, $\mathrm{{-}CO_2H}$, so it reacts with both acids and bases.

**(i) Equations.**

A- With nitric acid the amino group accepts a proton:

$\mathrm{CH_3CH(NH_2)CO_2H} + \mathrm{HNO_3} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH(NH_3^{+})CO_2H}\ \mathrm{NO_3^{-}}$

B- With sodium hydroxide the carboxyl group loses a proton:

$\mathrm{CH_3CH(NH_2)CO_2H} + \mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH(NH_2)CO_2^{-}Na^{+}} + \mathrm{H_2O}$

**(ii) At pH 7** (close to its isoelectric point, about 6) the acid exists as a **zwitterion**, the carboxyl group having transferred its proton to the amino group:

Structure: $\mathrm{CH_3CH(NH_3^{+})CO_2^{-}}$

Name: **zwitterion** (dipolar ion, internal salt).

**(iii) Stereoisomers.** Carbon 2 is bonded to four different groups ($\mathrm{{-}H}$, $\mathrm{{-}NH_2}$, $\mathrm{{-}CO_2H}$, $\mathrm{{-}CH_3}$), so the molecule is **chiral** and exists as a pair of **enantiomers** (optical isomers), mirror images that cannot be superimposed (Fischer projections):

```
         COOH                     COOH
          |                        |
  H2N --- C --- H          H --- C --- NH2
          |                        |
         CH3                      CH3
   L-(S)-2-aminopropanoic    D-(R)-2-aminopropanoic
          acid                     acid
```

The two forms rotate the plane of plane-polarised light by equal amounts in opposite directions; an equimolar mixture is optically inactive (racemic).
